In a study of coin images showing different sides, we explored a clustering challenge where not all classes are known in advance and appear in an unknown mix. The images' varied appearances, containing text and image imperfections, made traditional clustering methods challenging. Experiments indicated that standard methods performed poorly when encountered with unfamiliar data. A novel approach combining self-supervised and semi-supervised techniques enabled the discovery of a limited number of classes in the unseen data. However, the self-supervised method struggled to group the unseen classes together due to its reliance on optimized weights for known classes. A subsequent semi-supervised approach combined the self-supervised method with human-annotated labels for the unseen data, successfully training the model to recognize the hidden classes. These results demonstrate the potential for self-supervised methods to discover unknown data but highlight the need for human guidance to effectively identify all classes. To verify our findings, we conducted a follow-up study using a larger dataset of natural images with an unknown number of classes. This dataset allowed us to evaluate the robustness of self-supervised methods and compare their performance to supervised methods. Our experiments on ImageNet showed that self-supervised methods can achieve comparable results to supervised methods, but are more susceptible to noise. Moreover, the self-supervised methods are more resistant to adversarial attacks that target natural image distributions. These findings have implications for the self-supervised learning paradigm and the design of future self-supervised methods. Accurately predicting electricity demand and wind power production can greatly improve the management of power grids. Historically, the reliability of operating reserves has been determined using historical data on demand and wind generation, but this approach becomes less effective as forecasting technology advances. In this study, we explore a new method to calculate the minimum amount of reserve needed in power grids. Specifically, we developed a probabilistic approach to determining operating reserve requirements that takes into account the uncertainty surrounding future demand and wind output. By applying this approach to a data from Denmark, we found that incorporating forecast uncertainty into reserve requirements can significantly reduce the likelihood of power grid disruptions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model can be pre-trained on a small dataset, such as 100 portrait images, and fine-tuned for high-quality Neural Radiance Field reconstruction. Last-iterate convergence in games is a vital property. In adversarial games, it enables the identification of losing strategies, while cooperative games benefit from convergence to the Nash equilibrium. Researchers have established last-iterate convergence in zero-sum games over continuous action spaces, but the proof is missing for general-sum games over these spaces. Building upon a previously developed technique used in discrete action spaces, our research extends this approach to continuous action spaces. We demonstrate that regret minimization algorithms like regret matching and exponential gradient ascent exhibit last-iterate convergence in zero-sum games over continuous action spaces, and this finding also applies to general-sum games. Our work improves upon existing methods for approximating Nash equilibria in cooperative games and the exact equilibria in zero-sum games. We provide a theoretical framework for regret minimization algorithms and validate these concepts with empirical studies. The novel technique developed in this research can be applied to other algorithms in the field. Furthermore, our work also explores the convergence of last-iterate dynamics in general-sum games, and the existing theory is shown to be insufficient in this case. This results in planners producing trajectories that may be unfeasible or unstable, particularly in dynamic environments. In response, we propose a method for real-time motion planning that prioritizes the creation of trajectories that can be achieved seamlessly by the robot. This involves integrating information about the robot's motion capabilities into the motion planning process, along with details about the dynamics of the environment. Our approach is based on model predictive control, which is used to create real-time motion trajectories that can be executed in real-time, ultimately enabling the robot to navigate effectively in dynamic environments safely and efficiently. This method is demonstrated through a series of experiments conducted using a humanoid robot, which showcase its effectiveness in navigating environments with moving obstacles. Our results indicate that this approach successfully generates trajectories that can be executed in real-time, resulting in improved safety and feasibility. Additionally, we provide a comparison with a widely-used real-time motion planner, demonstrating that our method outperforms it in terms of producing stable and successful trajectories. This work represents a significant step towards developing a more robust and efficient method for real-time motion planning that prioritizes the execution capabilities of robots. In systems where molecules are connected through specific pathways, droplets can form and create temporary shortcuts that disrupt the direct path between distant molecules. By developing a model that takes into account these droplets, we investigated how they affect the way molecules are arranged in a system and how they impact long-distance relationships. Our analysis shows that when molecules are evenly distributed, the probability of finding two molecules separated by a distance increases at a slower rate than expected in models without droplets. Furthermore, the presence of droplets leads to a more rapid disconnection of molecules that are far apart, and this effect becomes more pronounced as the molecules are spread out. Additionally, the presence of droplets causes the average distance between molecules to increase more than predicted in a system without droplets. While our model was developed to describe self-avoiding walks, our findings also apply to percolation systems, as shown by comparing our model to simulations of percolation systems. Our results highlight the importance of considering temporary shortcuts in molecular models, particularly when studying large molecules that exhibit slow diffusion rates. This research aims to enhance speaker localization by leveraging external microphone data, resulting in more precise and efficient solutions. A proposed binary mask technique integrates information from external microphones with a neural network's feature map, ultimately improving time-delay estimation and thus speaker localization in complex, reverberant environments. When applied to a deep neural network (DNN)-based approach, this binary mask significantly reduces false positives by up to 52.5% on average. Notably, even a binary mask derived from a single external microphone produces notable improvements, with average reductions of up to 16.4% in false positives and up to 11.2% in false negatives. When applied to a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based approach, the binary mask leads to average reductions of up to 15.3% in false positives and up to 10.2% in false negatives. Experiment results, conducted in both simulated and real-world settings, demonstrate that the binary mask technique is a viable means of improving speaker localization using a DNN-based solution, or enhancing existing solutions by integrating external microphone data. This technique is particularly beneficial for applications in real-world scenarios where multiple microphones are readily available. This paper introduces Gemino, a novel video codec that utilizes temporal redundancy within each video frame to enhance efficiency. Gemino achieves this by partitioning each frame into various temporal sub-patches, each comprising a distinct temporal trajectory. In contrast to conventional video codecs that apply spatial and temporal prediction to entire frames, Gemino employs the spatial alignment of sub-patches to facilitate efficient temporal prediction, thus reducing the required bit stream and enabling the retention of high-quality video details, even at low bitrates. Our evaluation of Gemino on multiple video datasets demonstrates significant improvements over x264, averaging a 15.7% decrease in PsnR and 24.1% increase in SSIM at equivalent bit rates. Furthermore, our proposed approach is applicable to various video codec architectures, and the Gemino codebase is openly available on GitHub. https://github.com/VITA-HKR/Gemino. Our research tackles a significant challenge in garment manipulation: designing efficient manipulation policies for arbitrary garments that can be easily manipulated. Experimental results demonstrate that Graspy outperforms state-of-the-art policies in terms of manipulation success rate and average episode length. Additionally, the policy learnability and transferability evaluations confirm that Graspy's pre-processing policy generalizes well to various grasping and manipulation targets, making it more adaptable and efficient for simple manually-designed manipulation techniques.
